title: Pointers, Addresses and Pointer Declarations
learningObjectives: Explain how a pointer stores an object's address.
Declare typed pointers and initialize them safely.
Use address-of and dereference operators correctly.
Distinguish a pointer variable from its pointee.
Recognize uninitialized and invalid pointer risks.

understand.concept: A pointer variable stores an address of an object. The pointer type indicates the type of object it points to; use & to obtain an object's address.
understand.whyItMatters: Pointers are fundamental to APIs, dynamic objects, iterators and indirect access.
understand.explain: Initialize pointers, understand what object they refer to, and avoid invalid addresses.

examples.title: Address and pointer
examples.explanation: ptr stores the address of score.

examples.title: Typed pointer
examples.explanation: The pointer type matches the object type.

examples.title: Pointer initialized to null
examples.code: int* p=nullptr;\n// p currently points to no int object
examples.explanation: nullptr clearly represents an empty pointer.

examples.title: Change pointer target
examples.explanation: The pointer can be reassigned to another object of compatible type.

examples.title: Address operator
examples.code: int value=7;\nint* p=&value;\n*p=9; // value is now 9

practise.guidedTask: For Pointers, Addresses and Pointer Declarations, draw the object and pointer/reference relationships for every example. Mark owner, target, constness, lifetime, validity of access, and any operation that could invalidate the pointer or reference.
practise.independentTask: Write a focused C++ exercise for Pointers, Addresses and Pointer Declarations. Demonstrate at least three cases, including a safe usage and a boundary/invalid case explained in comments but not executed. State who owns the resource and when each object/view is valid.
hints: Draw the pointer/reference and its target object.
Mark whether the object is alive and who owns it.
Check nullptr and bounds before access.
Consider invalidation, deletion and scope exit.
Use standard containers or smart pointers when they express ownership more safely.
